## TL;DR

A wheel rolling without slipping has one special property: the point touching the ground is, for an instant, not moving relative to the ground at all. That kills the sliding-friction mechanism almost entirely. What's left, rolling resistance, is typically 50 to 400 times smaller than sliding friction for the same materials, which is most of why wheels exist. The remaining piece of the story, why a spinning wheel can lose grip, comes straight from [static friction beating kinetic](why-static-friction-beats-kinetic.qmd).
:::

## The contact point isn't moving

A wheel of radius $r$ rolling without slipping has its centre moving at speed $v$ while spinning at angular velocity $\omega = v/r$. Add the two motions at the point touching the ground, the forward velocity of the whole wheel and the backward velocity of that point as it rotates, and they cancel exactly: $v - \omega r = 0$. The contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the road.

That single fact (Figure 3) matters enormously, because the sliding friction described in the [previous module](why-static-friction-beats-kinetic.qmd) depends on surfaces continuously shearing fresh asperity junctions apart, which requires relative motion at the interface. A rolling wheel's contact patch has none. Drag a box and every asperity junction along the way gets sheared. Roll a wheel over the same ground and, ideally, no junction at the contact point is ever sheared at all, because that point never slides against the road while it's touching it.

Velocity grows linearly with height above the contact, from zero at the ground through $v$ at the axle to $2v$ at the top. ## What's left over, and how big it is

"Ideally" is doing work in that last sentence, and real wheels don't get away with zero resistance. Rolling resistance comes mostly from a different mechanism entirely: as a wheel bears load, it and the ground deform slightly ahead of the contact patch and spring back behind it, and if that material isn't perfectly elastic, some of the energy put into deforming it is lost as heat rather than returned, a hysteresis loss. A little more is lost to small amounts of micro-slip within a finite, not point-sized, contact patch and to adhesion at its leading and trailing edges. None of it involves the interface sliding wholesale the way a dragged block does. Figure 4 traces where the resistance actually comes from: the load ends up sitting slightly ahead of the axle rather than beneath it, by a distance $b$, and the torque that offset creates is what you have to overcome. Dividing through by the wheel radius gives $C_{rr} = b/r$, which is also the cleanest answer to why larger wheels roll more easily, since $b$ depends on how far the materials deform and not on how big the wheel is.

```{=html}
<figcaption><strong>Figure 4 | Rolling resistance comes from where the load sits, not from anything sliding.</strong> Under load the wheel and the surface deform, and because neither material returns quite all the energy it absorbed, the pressure on the leading half of the contact patch (blue) exceeds that on the trailing half. The resultant normal force $N$ therefore acts a small distance $b$ ahead of the axle instead of directly beneath it, and the torque $N b$ opposes rotation. Dividing by the wheel radius gives the resisting force, $F_{\text{roll}} = Nb/r = C_{rr}N$, which identifies the rolling resistance coefficient as simply $C_{rr} = b/r$. That ratio explains both the size of the effect and why a larger wheel rolls more easily over the same surface: $b$ is set by how much the materials deform, so a bigger $r$ divides it down.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


The force resisting rolling is written the same way sliding friction is, $F_{\text{roll}} = C_{rr} F_N$, but the rolling resistance coefficient $C_{rr}$ sits far below a typical sliding friction coefficient $\mu$:

| Contact | Sliding friction $\mu_k$ | Rolling resistance $C_{rr}$ | Rolling force as a share of sliding |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Rubber tyre on asphalt | $\approx 0.7$ | $\approx 0.012$ | $\approx 1.7\%$ |
| Steel wheel on steel rail | $\approx 0.57$ | $\approx 0.0015$ | $\approx 0.3\%$ |

Take those as representative, not exact: both $\mu$ and $C_{rr}$ shift with load, speed, temperature, tyre pressure and surface condition, and a soft, deformable surface like sand or loose soil behaves quite differently again. But the pattern is robust and large: rolling typically leaves you with somewhere between about $0.3\%$ and $2\%$ of the resistive force that sliding the same load over the same surface would cost, a reduction on the order of $98$ to $99.7\%$. That's the arithmetic behind why a train can move enormous freight loads on remarkably little power, and why the wheel, rather than a sled, is the default answer to "how do I move this heavy thing."

## Where the friction you didn't lose actually went

Cutting sliding friction to almost nothing sounds like a pure win, but a driven wheel, one an engine or a rider is actually turning to move forward, still needs friction, just not the kind that resists motion. Push torque through a powered wheel's axle and the tyre pushes backward on the road at the contact patch; by Newton's third law, the road pushes forward on the wheel with an equal and opposite force. That forward push is what accelerates the vehicle, and it is friction at a contact point that, as established above, is not sliding. It is static friction, and its ceiling is exactly the larger coefficient from the previous module: $F_{\max} = \mu_s F_N$.

This is where the two modules meet. As long as the torque demanded stays below what $\mu_s F_N$ can supply, the wheel grips and every bit of that torque becomes forward force. Push harder than that ceiling and the tyre starts to spin faster than $v = \omega r$ requires: the contact point is no longer at rest relative to the road, sliding friction takes over, and the force available drops to the smaller $\mu_k F_N$. Flooring the throttle from a stop on a low-traction surface doesn't just risk wasted effort, it can produce less forward force than a gentler push would have, precisely because it traded the larger static friction for the smaller kinetic one. Anti-lock braking and traction control systems exist to do one job: keep each wheel's contact patch right at the edge of slip, drawing on the largest friction available, static, without ever crossing into the smaller kind.

## Key takeaways

- A wheel rolling without slipping has zero relative velocity at its contact point, which avoids the continuous asperity-shearing that causes sliding friction almost entirely.
- What resistance remains, rolling resistance, comes mainly from hysteresis losses as the wheel and surface deform and spring back, not from sliding, and is typically 50 to 300 times smaller than sliding friction for comparable materials.
- Representative figures: a rubber tyre on asphalt keeps roughly $1$ to $2\%$ of the sliding-friction force as rolling resistance; a steel wheel on steel rail keeps roughly $0.3\%$.
- A driven or braked wheel still relies on friction, static friction at its contact patch, to convert torque into forward or stopping force, and its ceiling is the larger $\mu_s$, not the smaller $\mu_k$.
- Exceeding that ceiling makes the wheel slip, switching the contact from static to kinetic friction and reducing the available force, which is exactly why wheelspin costs traction rather than adding it.
